messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike, Robin,

I know this post is now a couple of years old, but I have had time to come back and revisit a problem identical to this one that I had during my PhD project. I had a similarly nested model comparing body shape across populations of fish from different habitat types (river/flowing vs reservoir/slow or no flow) and was running into the same issue of model comparions returning significant differences, but pairwise comparison in advanced.procd.lm yielding no significant differences between any groups. I was perplexed by this until by chance I found this post and attempted the comparison between a full and null model (no predictors), which yielded significant model-level differences and many significant pairwise differences.

The z-score as Mike suggested, gave it away when I looked at my initial, perplexing results. It seems that this may be a common situation with complex, multi-factorial cases where the organism or populations in question are not just different full stop, but rather differences are between specific groups (trait levels) within population (or species or other factor).

My dilemma, which I hope you can provide some advice on, is whether this is a publishable result? More specifically, I am not sure how to package the biological observation and the statistical anomaly that it gives rise to. Is this a characteristic of a multi-factorial problem where there is no one predictor (habitat type, sex and population) that strongly influences phenotypic divergence and complicates the statistical inference made from it? Or is it just an analytical quirk that editors will scoff at and pass off as statistical fluff? Has this been published on previously, and if so, is it something worth reporting again?

If nothing else I think it makes for an interesting aside and potentially provides two interesting results: 1) My study showed that phenotypic divergence was not attributable to any one predictor alone and morphological divergence in fish populations from low and high flow velocity habitats, may not be as clear cut as previous studies have shown, and 2) The statistical analysis can be very misleading, if not done with due care or passed off based on one measure of statistical difference.

I'd appreciate your thoughts and how you might suggest pitching this kind of result. I'm keen to report both outcomes, but I'm concerned they would come off as disjointed and distracting from one another.

I look forward to hearing from you and happy to discuss further if you are interested.

Regards,

Daniel

On Tuesday, 17 January 2017 02:36:13 UTC+11, Michael Collyer wrote:

> Dear Robin and all geomorph users,
>
> Robin’s issue of having a significant but small interaction effect, but also having no significant pairwise differences, got me to wondering how a type I error might manifest in terms of pairwise comparisons.  I decided to simulate data and run the same tests Robin performed.  I did two simulations: 1) where there were significant main effects, but no interaction and 2) where there were significant main effects plus a significant interaction.  When simulating data like these, in the case of the former, I could choose times when an interaction just happened to be significant, even though it should not be.  This is a type I error (just from random sampling).  In each case that this happened, the effect was small but significant, and when I ran advanced.procD.lm for pairwise comparisons, none were significant, just like Robin found.  When I simulated a meaningful interaction, the interaction was significant each time, and some pairwise comparisons were also significant.
>
> There is a lesson to learn here.
>
> Hinging inferences on P-values from results is dangerous.  This might be especially true for highly multivariate data.  In Robin’s case, she found that an interaction that explained 1.5% of the shape variation was “significant”.  That means that in the 1000 permutations she used, never was there SS for the interaction that exceeded her observed case.  But that does not mean the SS was large.  This is why we provide Rsq and effect sizes (Z scores) for all of our statistics.  It allows one to use multiple criteria for deciding if a result is biologically significant, rather than merely statistically significant.
>
> Another, more simple analogy to consider this problem is to think of size, not shape.  Let’s say hypothetically that females are just slightly smaller in Robin’s A group and just slightly larger than males in her T group.  In each case, there is not sexual dimorphism.  But these small, but not significant effects could combine to produce a small but significant sex x ancestry effect, even though no pairwise comparisons are significant.  (This problem might be exacerbated with many shape variables.)
>
> Finally, Robin, it is worth pointing out that you performed a test with ~ ancestry + sex as the null model.  This means you did not find any significant pairwise differences with respect to general factor-level differences.  For example, sexual dimorphism in A and T groups were both no different than sexual dimorphism for both groups combined.  If you had just used an intercept as a null model (~ 1), you would surely find significant pairwise distances.  So your result does not mean there is not significant sexual dimorphism; it just means that the sexual dimorphisms in each group do not differ from overall sexual dimorphism.
>
> I hope that helps wrap up this analytical paradox for you.
>
> Cheers!
> Mike

Hi Daniel,

You might want to check the geomorph google group archives, as we has a similar discussion at the end of October; see “pairwise function and RRPP procedure”.

I’ll reiterate what I said in that discussion.  One should indicate the null model used for the hypothesis test.  To suggest that one is testing the null hypothesis, var(population means) = 0 is only partly informative.  There are multiple hypothesis tests that look similar but can yield quite different results; i.e.,

var(population means) | overall mean = 0
var(population means) | habitat type = 0

The condition in the statements above is the null model used to generate sampling differences of pairwise differences among means.  I think it is appropriate to do both tests and report results for both tests.  The former asks if the means are different; the latter asks if the means are different, given differences in habitat types.  It is possible that both tests yield “significant” results but one (perhaps the latter) does not identify meaningful pairwise differences, based on effect sizes.

There is no limit for the pairwise tests that can be performed.  One can do pairwise tests for, e.g.,

var(B levels) | A

and

var(A levels) | B

The way I would pitch it is explicitly defining what the null model is when I do my pairwise test, and if I have multiple tests, I would define the null model in each case.  I believe the tests should be disarticulated if doing multiple tests for comparison of the same means, and defined.  I believe they become “disjointed” if it is not clear to the person reading the results how the tests are different but both important.

Hope that helps - Mike

messages.subject: Question about estimating missing LMs
messages.body_plain:
I have a question about the estimate.missing function. I am working with artifacts (spear points) that often are broken at their extremities, most often their tips and sometimes their ears. I want to compare the ability of the regression option (tps, too) to predict the missing tips and ears with the abilities of individual archaeologist-analysts. I also want to see the results by placing the predicted LMs on an image to understand the nature of the predictions (for example, when they err, the analysts tend to predict the tip was longer than it actually is).

To do so, I convert landmarks for 68 images, with missing data for tips on four images and ears on two others to NA and run the estimate.missing function with the following code:

APTM<-readland.tps("APtestImages.tps", specID=c("ID"))

APTM[5,,65]<-APTM[5,,66]<-APTM[5,,68]<-APTM[5,,69]<-NA

APTM[3,,64]<-APTM[3,,67]<-NA

APTM.reg<-estimate.missing(APTM,method="Reg")

It works! I do the R dance of happiness.

But my happiness is shortlived. I want to replace the NA values in the original data set with the regression-estimated LMs to determine how well the regression estimated the tips and ears for those points. I can do that with the analyst-predictions, but I also want to do this with the regression (and tps) predicted LMs. Alas, all the regression LMs are very different (many are now negative numbers). I can discern no relationship between the actual LM locations and the regression results, but assume they are perhaps centered and standardized.  Is there a way a mere mortal could convert the regression results back to the scale of the original data?

Is there a way to do this?

Thanks,

Dave Thulman

during estimate.missing, the data are superimposed, in order to be able to estimate the positions of the missing landmarks accurately.

I think the fastest way for you to do what you want is to take the original (full) data for your specimens for which you are creating missing landmarks, and the new (estimated) ones, and superimpose them again, to put them in a coherent shape space.

Not sure this is what you are trying to do, though... Hope this helps.

Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
Dave,

There are two algorithms that can be used. From the help file:

The first approach (method="TPS") uses the thin-plate spline to interpolate landmarks on a reference specimen to estimate the locations of missing landmarks on a target specimen. Here, a reference specimen is obtained from the set of specimens for which all landmarks are present, Next, each incomplete specimen is aligned to the reference using the set of landmarks common to both. Finally, the thin-plate spline is used to estimate the locations of the missing landmarks in the target specimen (Gunz et al. 2009).

The second approach (method="Reg") is multivariate regression. Here each landmark with missing values is regressed on all other landmarks for the set of complete specimens, and the missing landmark values are then predicted by this linear regression model. Because the number of variables can exceed the number of specimens, the regression is implemented on scores along the first set of PLS axes for the complete and incomplete blocks of landmarks (see Gunz et al. 2009).

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Question about estimating missing LMs
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Dean,
What I want to do is take the new, estimated LM of the artifact tip and place it on the original specimen image to compare it to the location of the actual tip. Because my original LM data was created using tpsDIG2, all the LM locations are positive numbers. In my case I used 62 reference images and 6 images with single missing LMs. For example, LM5 (the tip LM) on the actual image is at location 586, 1215, but in the regression it is 6.4348757.

Does this make sense?
Dave

>
>
>

>
>
>
> The first approach (method="TPS") uses the thin-plate spline to interpolate landmarks on a reference specimen to estimate the locations of missing landmarks on a target specimen. Here, a reference specimen is obtained from the set of specimens for which all landmarks are present, Next, each incomplete specimen is aligned to the reference using the set of landmarks common to both. Finally, the thin-plate spline is used to estimate the locations of the missing landmarks in the target specimen (Gunz et al. 2009).
>
> The second approach (method="Reg") is multivariate regression. Here each landmark with missing values is regressed on all other landmarks for the set of complete specimens, and the missing landmark values are then predicted by this linear regression model. Because the number of variables can exceed the number of specimens, the regression is implemented on scores along the first set of PLS axes for the complete and incomplete blocks of landmarks (see Gunz et al. 2009).
>
> Dean
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Two years ago, I was visiting my mother in law and tried to dash off a quick response to one of these threads in morphmet, making a number of mistakes for which I had to atone. Here I am visiting her again, taking the same risk.

If the missing landmark is LmX, then after estimating LmX you have S1 (the true, complete specimen in its original location) and S1X (S1 with LmX knocked out, then estimated). LmC are all landmarks in the configuration other than LmX, i.e., those shared in common by S1 and S1X. It's hacky, but couldn't you...
Rescale S1X by the scaling factor required to make S1X[LmC] the same centroid size as S1[LmC].
Translate S1X so that the centroid of S1X[LmC] is in the same location as the centroid of S1[LmC].
Use the procOPA function from the shapes package to obtain the rotation matrix that rotates S1X[LmC] to S1[LmC]. RM <- procOPA(A=S1[LmC], B=S1X[LmC], scale = FALSE, reflect = FALSE)$R
Note that because S1X[LmC] and S1[LmC] are identical configurations after step 2, you have just created a rotation matrix to rotate a configuration to itself. The fit will be perfect for the LmC landmarks.
Apply RM to the entire S1X configuration. I think it's S1X_R <- S1X %*% RM, but it could require t(RM). Somebody please chime in here.
Now compare the positions of S1X_R[LmX] to S1[LmX].
Hopefully I haven't left anything out. The problem with this approach is that if there is any actual rescaling that occurs in step 1, you have changed the regression estimate of your incomplete configuration. Whether a rescaling has occurred depends on how the estimate.missing routine works. Having said that, you don't necessarily want a missing landmark estimation strategy that changes the shape or size of the configuration for the landmarks that are not missing.

Best, David

David,

The scaling won’t be the same because each is based on a different number of landmarks. One would need to find the Csize of those landmarks other than the missing one and use that.

I guess what I don’t get is why one wishes to do this when several vetted landmark estimation methods exist.

Subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Question about estimating missing LMs

Hi everyone,

Two years ago, I was visiting my mother in law and tried to dash off a quick response to one of these threads in morphmet, making a number of mistakes for which I had to atone. Here I am visiting her again, taking the same risk.

If the missing landmark is LmX, then after estimating LmX you have S1 (the true, complete specimen in its original location) and S1X (S1 with LmX knocked out, then estimated). LmC are all landmarks in the configuration other than LmX, i.e., those shared in common by S1 and S1X. It's hacky, but couldn't you...
Rescale S1X by the scaling factor required to make S1X[LmC] the same centroid size as S1[LmC].
Translate S1X so that the centroid of S1X[LmC] is in the same location as the centroid of S1[LmC].
Use the procOPA function from the shapes package to obtain the rotation matrix that rotates S1X[LmC] to S1[LmC]. RM <- procOPA(A=S1[LmC], B=S1X[LmC], scale = FALSE, reflect = FALSE)$R
Note that because S1X[LmC] and S1[LmC] are identical configurations after step 2, you have just created a rotation matrix to rotate a configuration to itself. The fit will be perfect for the LmC landmarks.
Apply RM to the entire S1X configuration. I think it's  S1X_R <- S1X %*% RM, but it could require t(RM). Somebody please chime in here.
Now compare the positions of S1X_R[LmX] to S1[LmX].

Hopefully I haven't left anything out. The problem with this approach is that if there is any actual rescaling that occurs in step 1, you have changed the regression estimate of your incomplete configuration. Whether a rescaling has occurred depends on how the estimate.missing routine works. Having said that, you don't necessarily want a missing landmark estimation strategy that changes the shape or size of the configuration for the landmarks that are not missing.

Best, David

I can think of 2 reasons. The tips on these artifacts are variable (Likely more so than a typical biological specimen), sometimes pointy, sometimes rounded, sometimes offset, etc.
First, I'm interested in whether the regression has a systematic error (assuming it has an error). The analysts' estimates showed they estimated long in 4 of 6 efforts (2 were spot on).If I find that the errors occurred more often with certain kinds of tips (say rounded, rather than pointy), I could decide just to delete rounded-tipped points.
Second, I want to see what the absolute error is. The analysts' errors were no more than 1.2 mm off, but I don't know what the magnitude of the regression error is. This is more than curiosity, because even if regression is relatively better than estimating as measured by Procrustes distance, if the magnitude of the error is significant (however significance is defined), then it may be better to simply delete specimens.

Does this make sense?

Dave Thulman

messages.body_plain:
Dave,

The only way to know the components you wish (magnitude of error and directional bias) is to perform a simulation study on your particular objects. Specifically, one uses a set of ‘true’ specimens were all landmarks are found, and then create specimens with missing landmarks by deleting them. Then one uses various methods for estimating the positions of those landmarks and compares the estimated values to the true ones.

This is precisely the procedure used in the two studies I am aware of that compare missing landmark estimation methods: one published (Arbour and Brown 2014), and one not (https://www.virtual-anthropology.com/virtual-anthropology/reconstruct/reference-based-reconstruction/). And, this is what I do in our workshops when we discuss missing landmark approaches.

Most frequently, it is found that regression is generally the more robust procedure, though the extent of difference between methods can change somewhat in magnitude (not surprisingly) by the shape of the structure, the number of landmarks being estimated, where on the structure the missing landmarks were found, etc.

My suggestion is that you conduct such a study to determine the extent of error and/or bias in estimating the tip points when using TPS, regression or other approaches.

Simulations with known results are always the way to go for evaluating methods, IMO.

I thought David T's purpose was to "place [the imputed tip] on the original specimen image to compare it to the location of the actual tip," which at a minimum has some qualitative inference value.

> The only way to know the components you wish (magnitude of error and directional bias) is to perform a simulation study on your particular objects. Specifically, one uses a set of ‘true’ specimens were all landmarks are found, and then create specimens with missing landmarks by deleting them. Then one uses various methods for estimating the positions of those landmarks and compares the estimated values to the true ones.
>
>
>

And, this is what I do in our workshops when we discuss missing landmark approaches.
>
>
>
> Most frequently, it is found that regression is generally the more robust procedure, though the extent of difference between methods can change somewhat in magnitude (not surprisingly) by the shape of the structure, the number of landmarks being estimated, where on the structure the missing landmarks were found, etc.
>
>
>
> My suggestion is that you conduct such a study to determine the extent of error and/or bias in estimating the tip points when using TPS, regression or other approaches.
>
>
>
> Simulations with known results are always the way to go for evaluating methods, IMO.

messages.body_plain:
David K is correct. I would like to look at individual specimens, because each will have peculiarities that might be informative.

On Fri, Dec 13, 2019 at 4:59 PM David K <katz...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I thought David T's purpose was to "place [the imputed tip] on the original specimen image to compare it to the location of the actual tip," which at a minimum has some qualitative inference value.
>
> On Fri, Dec 13, 2019 at 2:18 PM Adams, Dean [EEOB] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:
> >
> > Dave,
> >
> >
> >
> > The only way to know the components you wish (magnitude of error and directional bias) is to perform a simulation study on your particular objects. Specifically, one uses a set of ‘true’ specimens were all landmarks are found, and then create specimens with missing landmarks by deleting them. Then one uses various methods for estimating the positions of those landmarks and compares the estimated values to the true ones.
> >
> >
> >
> > This is precisely the procedure used in the two studies I am aware of that compare missing landmark estimation methods: one published (Arbour and Brown 2014), and one not (https://www.virtual-anthropology.com/virtual-anthropology/reconstruct/reference-based-reconstruction/). And, this is what I do in our workshops when we discuss missing landmark approaches.
> >
> >
> >
> > Most frequently, it is found that regression is generally the more robust procedure, though the extent of difference between methods can change somewhat in magnitude (not surprisingly) by the shape of the structure, the number of landmarks being estimated, where on the structure the missing landmarks were found, etc.
> >
> >
> >

> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The first approach (method="TPS") uses the thin-plate spline to interpolate landmarks on a reference specimen to estimate the locations of missing landmarks on a target specimen. Here, a reference specimen is obtained from the set of specimens for which all landmarks are present, Next, each incomplete specimen is aligned to the reference using the set of landmarks common to both. Finally, the thin-plate spline is used to estimate the locations of the missing landmarks in the target specimen (Gunz et al. 2009).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The second approach (method="Reg") is multivariate regression. Here each landmark with missing values is regressed on all other landmarks for the set of complete specimens, and the missing landmark values are then predicted by this linear regression model. Because the number of variables can exceed the number of specimens, the regression is implemented on scores along the first set of PLS axes for the complete and incomplete blocks of landmarks (see Gunz et al. 2009).

messages.body_plain:
Ok.  It seems the email thread has managed to intertwine two separate issues: one of determining which method of estimating landmarks is ‘best’ for a particular problem, with one of investigating the missing landmarks in a particular dataset.  For the former, I contend that the pathway I described is the only valid one as far as I am aware (i.e., compare methods with known data that are made to be missing via simulation.).

For the latter, I think these are the following steps (though I might have missed some as this thread has become somewhat circuitous):

1: estimate missing landmarks with some method

2: re-scale specimens (using the non-missing landmarks), so the original and estimated have the same size

3: re-rotate and re-orient the two so these landmarks perfectly align (which they should).

What is left is the estimated landmark.

Now, if one wishes to try and put that back in ‘pixel units’ there is yet another step that requires additional adjustment (i.e., finding the pixel to mm scale, and running that math backwards).

I hope this helps.

Yes, that definitely clears. But I don't think what you want is possible with individual species gpas because

1. If your species have different set of landmarks, then the dimensionality of covariance matrices will be different, eigenvectors have different lengths.
2. Each PCA will be centered around the species mean gpa is conducted on, so the scores will loose their meaning when you try concatenate results across different analysis.

Is there a reason you cannot combine your all your species in the same GPA? Different number or configuration of landmarks?

messages.subject_clean: new versions of RRPP and geomorph available
messages.body_plain:
Colleagues,

CRAN will soon release R 4.0, and in anticipation of this change, we have made several updates to both geomorph and RRPP to be compliant.  We also took the opportunity to clean up some bugs and make some minor adjustments.

In terms of new functionality, geomorph now contains multivariate effect sizes in the output of functions for which they are relevant (i.e., integration and modularity methods, PLS, phylogenetic signal, and evolutionary rates functions). Additionally, within RRPP the ‘classify’ function has been deprecated in favor of a new function, ‘prep.lda’, which sets things up for an lda analysis.

As always specific changes are specified in the news files. Users should be sure to investigate both help files, and the vignettes that accompany the programs, for proper usage.

Best to all.

Dean, Mike, and Antigoni (the geomorph team)

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Director of Graduate Education, EEB Program

Professor

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

https://www.eeob.iastate.edu/faculty/adams/

phone: 515-294-3834
